drivingQuestion: In what way does the verse exempt one engaged in a mitzva and a groom, and why is one who marries a widow not exempt?
outcomeNote: This unit opens with מאי משמע on the baraita cited in berakhot.sugya133 and has no antecedent of its own; the chain of difficulties ends with the distinction between voluntary and mitzva preoccupation.

segments.he: מַאי מַשְׁמַע? אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: כִּי דֶרֶךְ. מָה דֶּרֶךְ רְשׁוּת, אַף הָכָא נָמֵי רְשׁוּת.
segments.en: The Gemara clarifies the meaning of this baraita, and asks: «From where is it inferred» that the verse: “When you walk along the way,” enables us to derive that a groom is exempt from the obligation to recite Shema? «Rav Pappa said» that it is derived: «Like the way; just as» the journey along a specific «way» described in the verse «is voluntary» and involves no mitzva, «so too all» of those who are obligated to recite Shema are engaged in «voluntary activities.» However, one engaged in performance of a mitzva is exempt from the obligation to recite Shema.

segments.he: מִי לָא עָסְקִינַן דְּקָאָזֵיל לִדְבַר מִצְוָה, וַאֲפִילּוּ הָכִי אָמַר רַחֲמָנָא: לִיקְרֵי.
segments.en: The Gemara asks: «Are we not dealing with» a case where one is walking along «on his way to» perform «a mitzva; nevertheless, the Torah said to recite» Shema, indicating that he is obligated even if he set out to perform a mitzva.

segments.he: אִם כֵּן, לֵימָא קְרָא ״בְּלֶכֶת״, מַאי ״בְּלֶכְתְּךָ״ — שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ: בְּלֶכֶת דִּידָךְ הוּא דִּמְחַיְּיבַתְּ, הָא דְמִצְוָה — פְּטִירַתְּ.
segments.en: The Gemara explains: «If so,» that the intention was to obligate in all cases, «let the Torah say: When walking» along the way. «What is» the meaning of: «When you walk» along the way? «Conclude from this: It is» in a case «of your walking,» meaning that when you do this for your own purposes and of your own volition, «you are obligated» to recite Shema, «but» when you go with the objective «of» performing a «mitzva, you are exempt.»

segments.he: אִי הָכִי מַאי אִירְיָא הַכּוֹנֵס אֶת הַבְּתוּלָה? אֲפִילּוּ כּוֹנֵס אֶת הָאַלְמָנָה נָמֵי.
segments.en: The Gemara questions this: «If so, why discuss» a case of «one who is marrying a virgin» in particular? «Even one who is marrying a widow» is performing a mitzva and should «also» be exempt.

The Gemara responds that nevertheless, there is a distinction between one marrying a virgin and one marrying a widow. «Here,» in the case of one who marries a virgin, the groom is «preoccupied» by his thoughts, «while here,» in the case of one who marries a widow, «he is not preoccupied.»

segments.he: אִי מִשּׁוּם טִרְדָּא, אֲפִילּוּ טָבְעָה סְפִינָתוֹ בַּיָּם נָמֵי, אַלְּמָה אָמַר רַבִּי אַבָּא בַּר זַבְדָּא אָמַר רַב: אָבֵל חַיָּיב בְּכָל מִצְוֹת הָאֲמוּרוֹת בַּתּוֹרָה, חוּץ מִן הַתְּפִילִּין שֶׁהֲרֵי נֶאֱמַר בָּהֶן ״פְּאֵר״, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״פְּאֵרְךָ חֲבוֹשׁ עָלֶיךָ וְגוֹ׳״!
segments.en: The Gemara challenges: «If» a groom is exempt from the recitation of Shema simply «due to preoccupation,» then «even» one who is preoccupied because «his ship sank at sea should» be exempt. If so, «why then did Rabbi Abba bar Zavda say» that «Rav said: A mourner is obligated in all the mitzvot mentioned in the Torah except for» the mitzva to don «phylacteries, as» the term «splendor is stated» with regard to phylacteries, «as it is stated» that the prophet Ezekiel was prohibited to mourn and was told: «“Bind your splendor upon yourself”» (Ezekiel 24:17). If even a mourner, who is pained and preoccupied, is obligated to recite Shema, clearly preoccupation has no bearing upon one’s obligation.

segments.he: אָמְרִי הָתָם טִרְדָּא דִרְשׁוּת הָכָא טִרְדָּא דְמִצְוָה.
segments.en: The Gemara responds: Nevertheless, there is a distinction between the cases. «There,» it is a case of «preoccupation with a voluntary» act, as there is no mitzva to be preoccupied with his mourning, but «here,» in the case of a groom, the cause of «the preoccupation is» the «mitzva» itself.

moves.summary: how does 'when you walk along the way' imply the groom's exemption?
moves.about: in what way the words 'when you walk along the way' yield the groom's exemption

moves.summary: as the 'way' of the verse is voluntary, so the obligation attaches only to voluntary activity
moves.about: the verse's 'way' is a voluntary journey, so only voluntary activity carries the obligation

moves.cueHe: מי לא עסקינן דקאזיל לדבר מצוה
moves.summary: the verse's own case includes one walking to a mitzva, and he was still commanded to recite
moves.about: the verse's 'way' covers one walking to perform a mitzva, and the Torah still commanded him to recite

moves.summary: then the verse should have said belekhet; the possessive belekhtekha is what restricts it
moves.about: the verse's possessive wording, not the bare word 'way', is what restricts the obligation to one's own journey

moves.cueHe: שמע מינה: בלכת דידך הוא דמחייבת
moves.summary: hence you are obligated on your own journey and exempt on a mitzva journey
moves.about: had the obligation been unrestricted the verse would have said belekhet rather than belekhtekha

moves.cueHe: אי הכי מאי איריא הכונס את הבתולה?
moves.summary: then one who marries a widow, also engaged in a mitzva, should be exempt as well
moves.about: if the exemption follows from being engaged in a mitzva, one who marries a widow is equally engaged in a mitzva and should be exempt too

moves.summary: the one marrying a virgin is preoccupied, the one marrying a widow is not
moves.about: one who marries a virgin is preoccupied while one who marries a widow is not

moves.cueHe: אי משום טרדא, אפילו טבעה ספינתו בים נמי
moves.summary: preoccupation alone cannot be the ground, since a mourner is obligated in all the mitzvot
moves.about: if preoccupation alone exempts, one whose ship sank should be exempt, yet a mourner is obligated in all mitzvot

moves.summary: the mourner's preoccupation is voluntary; the groom's arises from the mitzva itself
moves.about: the mourner's preoccupation is with a voluntary matter while the groom's arises from the mitzva itself
